title: The rise and fall of language diversity through the Holocene.
data_url: https://zenodo.org/records/20042295 (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20042295, CC-BY-4.0); code repository at https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/NEUTV

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded and parsed all 6 files of the Zenodo deposit (2.66 MB total). dplace_paleoling.xlsx: 339 rows x 48 columns, one sheet, 293 unique Glottolog language codes (46 duplicated), columns include Population of ethnic group (339 non-null, 249 distinct values), endangerment 'status' (safe 132 / critically endangered 70 / extinct 57 / vulnerable 29 / severely endangered 27 / definitely endangered 24), Forager (209 yes / 130 no), Fishing percentage, Mobility, Contact, latitude/longitude, ISO 639-3 code, language family. glottolog_nov19.csv: 24,701 rows x 15 columns, 8,014 rows with an ISO 639-3 code, 8,301 with coordinates, and two columns ('description', 'markup_description') entirely empty; no endangerment or speaker-count column. meta_data_autotyp.txt: 2,950 rows x 25 columns, 2,705 unique Glottolog codes, Subsistence missing for 2,237 of 2,950 rows (76%). popc_r.txt plus lower/upper bound versions: each 28 rows (27 world regions + a Total row) x 76 year columns spanning 10,000 BCE to 2017 CE, values are population counts with no units row or data dictionary.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The abstract only; Science is not open access and there is no PMC record, so I never saw the methods, the data availability statement or the supplementary materials. The claim that 27 regional paleodemographic curves were fed into a simulation producing tens of thousands of languages 3,000-1,000 years ago comes from the abstract and the press coverage, not from any file. The OSF code repository (OSF.IO/NEUTV) returned HTTP 503 on four attempts via both the API and the web path, so I could not confirm whether it holds extra files; I treat it as unavailable.

a1_downloadable.note: Zenodo record 20042295 is fully open under CC-BY-4.0; I downloaded all six files directly, no login. The linked OSF code repository was down (HTTP 503) but is not needed for the data.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: The paper's quantity of interest, the number of languages alive in a region at a given date, is nowhere a column; it is produced by the authors' simulation. The deposit holds only its inputs. A target would have to be constructed, or borrowed from a different database.

a3_inputs_present.note: Features are present as values: latitude/longitude, language family, subsistence percentages, mobility and population are all in the spreadsheet; Glottolog codes and ISO 639-3 codes are present for joining.

a4_units_stated.note: The population curve files (popc_r.txt and its lower/upper bounds) have a bare region column and year headers only, with no units row and no data dictionary; magnitude implies persons but it is never stated. The spreadsheet's 'Fishing' column is a bare number (percentage of diet implied by the Binford variable name).

a5_enough_rows.note: The only table with measured outcomes is the 339-society spreadsheet, below the 1,500-row bar for regression and below the 400-row bar even for classification. The 24,701-row Glottolog dump is a public reference list with no outcome column, and the population curves are 28 rows x 76 years.

a6_fits_laptop.note: Whole deposit loads into memory instantly; no GPU, no streaming needed.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Nothing contradicts the abstract, but I could not check counts against the methods because the paper is paywalled and absent from PubMed Central.

a8_label_provenance.note: The headline trajectories are simulation output, so training on them would distil the authors' own model rather than learn anything measured. The population curves are themselves the output of paleodemographic reconstruction models, not census measurements, so they are model predictions too.

existing_models.name: Predicting Language Endangerment: A Machine Learning Approach (IEEE ICCCNT 2020 conference paper)
existing_models.score_and_split: Not retrieved. I saw only the title, venue and an abstract snippet in search results, not the paper, so I record no number.

integration.partner_dataset: Glottolog (current release, which carries Agglomerated Endangerment Status) and Grambank (~400,000 grammatical feature values for ~2,400 languages)
integration.join_key: Glottocode (an 8-character Glottolog language identifier) or ISO 639-3 code, both present in the files
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Which languages are at risk, given geography, family and neighbours — but this question is answerable from Glottolog and Grambank alone, so this paper's deposit adds nothing to it.

controls.positive_control: Predict latitude from the region code, which must be near-perfect; or recover the known association between foraging subsistence and small group size.
controls.negative_control: Shuffle the Population column and confirm collapse to the global mean.
controls.external_validation: None within this deposit; the current Glottolog release would be an outside source, but it replaces rather than validates these files.

honest_claim_h3: At best: 'among 339 hunter-gatherer societies that twentieth-century ethnographers happened to describe, ethnic-group size can be predicted from subsistence, mobility and location' — a claim about a small, old, heavily Western-North-America-weighted ethnographic convenience sample, not about languages through the Holocene.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a society's location, food sources and mobility to predict how many people speak its language.
plain_idea.train_on: One spreadsheet of 339 hunter-gatherer societies, each with latitude and longitude, language family, how much of the diet comes from fishing, whether the group is mobile or settled, and whether it is still a forager.
plain_idea.predict: The size of the ethnic group in people. The true value comes from Lewis Binford's compilation of twentieth-century ethnographic reports, each entry traced to published fieldwork with a focal year.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Researchers who model how languages split and die need a rule for how big a speaker community is; right now they assume one. But 339 rows is far too few to learn that rule, and the data is a convenience sample of whoever ethnographers visited.

more_or_better_data.why: The deposit is 2.66 MB and contains no new measurements: a 2019 Glottolog dump, an AUTOTYP metadata table, Binford's 339-society compilation and 28 regional population curves, all of which existed before this paper.

confidence_score.why: There are no replicate measurements. The population curves ship lower and upper bound files, but those are the authors' scenario bounds, not repeated observations of anything.

models_beatable.why: The paper's contribution is an agent-based simulation of language birth and death, not a predictor with a test-set number, so there is no score to beat and no honest split to re-run.

guaranteed_improvement.why: No baseline can be run on our side and there is no held-out evaluation to share; the simulation's output cannot be checked against any measured count of ancient languages.

ml_idea: The only supervised task the files support is predicting hunter-gatherer group size or endangerment status from geography, subsistence and mobility across 339 societies. That is a small-n statistics exercise, not a machine learning project, and the interesting version of it (predicting endangerment for all ~8,000 living languages) is served by Glottolog and Grambank directly, without this paper.

effort.compute_note: Measured file sizes directly: 2.66 MB total, all six files parsed in under a second with pandas on this laptop. Effort is trivially low; the problem is that there is nothing to model.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count the rows in dplace_paleoling.xlsx. It is 339, which kills it in one command.

verdict_reason: Fails A5 outright: the single table with measured outcomes has 339 rows, below the 400-row floor for even a classification task, and the other files are a public Glottolog dump with no outcome column plus a 28-row population grid. It also fails A2 and A8, because the paper's quantity of interest (number of languages alive at a given date) is simulation output rather than a column, and the population curves it rests on are themselves paleodemographic model predictions, so training on them would distil the authors' model instead of learning from measurements. A4 fails too: the population files carry no units anywhere. Secondarily, this is historical linguistics, outside the project's biology-only scope, and the only genuinely large resource it touches (Glottolog) is freely available without reference to this paper.
